blocks.text: 2.1.4 Inheritance Basics in Java

`PremiumAccount extends Account` and redeclares `overdraftLimit` as 5,000, yet premium customers are refused once they are 1,000 overdrawn. Next to it, a `TreeSet` subclass that counts additions for a dashboard counts six when three cities are added from a `List`, and three when they come as a `TreeSet`. Neither subclass has a line that looks wrong. Each assumes something about its superclass that isn't so.
Dispatch, static hiding and private methods are unit 1.3.1; covariant returns are unit 1.3.2.
A Field Is Hidden, Not Overridden: the Declared Type Picks Which One Is Read
With `Account asAccount = premium`, predict the three lines, then read them:

premium.overdraftLimit:   5000
asAccount.overdraftLimit: 1000
premium.canWithdraw(3_000): false

A premium account has two fields named `overdraftLimit`. Only overridable instance methods are chosen by the object at run time. The compiler binds a field access to the field of the declared type, and inside `Account` that type is `Account`, so `canWithdraw` reads 1,000 whatever the object is. A test that checks `premium.overdraftLimit` passes, and customers are refused.
Put the varying value behind a method the subclass overrides:
Now `canWithdraw(3_000)` on a premium account returns `true`.
<!-- practice 1 -->
super.m() Calls the Superclass's Version, and Nothing Reaches Past It
An audit logger extends a JSON logger and wants `Logger`'s plain text. Calling `format("card blocked")` on it:
AuditLogger: java.lang.StackOverflowError

A cast changes the declared type, not the object, so the call dispatches to `AuditLogger.format` again, which calls itself. `super.format(msg)` would print `AUDIT {"msg":"card blocked"}`: a `super` call is not dispatched on the object. It runs the version the direct superclass has, declared there or inherited, here `JsonLogger`'s. `super.super.format(msg)` doesn't compile (`<identifier> expected`).
Once `JsonLogger` overrides `format`, no subclass of `JsonLogger` can reach `Logger`'s version. If the plain version is needed, `JsonLogger` must offer it under another name.
Code Called Through super Still Calls Your Overrides, So a Subclass Depends on Its Superclass's Self-Calls
The dashboard's set counts in both methods:

addAll(a List) on an empty set:       6
addAll(a TreeSet) on an empty set:    3
then, on that set, addAll(2 more):    7

`super.addAll(c)` runs `TreeSet`'s code, but on this object, and the calls that code makes to `add` are ordinary virtual calls that reach `CountingSet.add`. For a `List`, `TreeSet.addAll` adds the elements one by one through `add`. For a sorted set with the same ordering, added to an empty set, it builds the tree directly and calls no `add` at all. Removing the `addAll` override ("it calls `add` anyway") gives:

addAll(a List) on an empty set:       3
addAll(a TreeSet) on an empty set:    0

None of this is in `TreeSet`'s javadoc, so a later JDK may change which method calls which, and the counts change without a compile error. This is the fragile base class problem: a subclass that overrides a method its superclass calls on itself depends on the superclass's implementation, not its contract.

Wrap the set and forward to it instead, so its internal calls never reach your code (unit 8.4.1 develops this). Or, for a class you write to be extended, document which methods call which and make the rest `final`.
<!-- practice 2 -->
An Override Can Widen Access but Not Narrow It, So a Subclass Can't Take a Method Away
An escrow account must not be closed by hand, so its author tries to hide `close()`:

A caller holding an `Account` compiled against a public `close()` and gets the escrow override at run time. Access is checked against the declared type, so a narrower override couldn't keep anyone out. Leaving out `@Override` changes nothing: the method still overrides, and the same error follows. Widening is allowed: `Object.clone()` is `protected`, `ArrayList.clone()` is `public`.

That leaves an override that throws. It compiles, and the failure moves to run time: a loop that closes three accounts closes the first, throws at the escrow one, and never reaches the third. Code written against `Account` breaks: the Liskov principle, unit 8.1.3.
protected Reaches a Subclass in Another Package Only Through Its Own Type

premium/PremiumAccount.java:8: error: balance has protected access in Account
    void absorb(Account other) { balance += other.balance; }
                                                 ^
1 error

Outside `bank`, `PremiumAccount` may use `balance` only through references of type `PremiumAccount` or its subclasses. Otherwise any class could read any account's balance by declaring a subclass. Inside `bank`, every class reads `balance` freely: `protected` includes package access, so it exposes more than package-private does.
<!-- practice 3 -->
Summary

items: **Fields are hidden, not overridden.** Code in the superclass reads its own field; vary a value through an overridable method.
**`super.m()` runs the direct superclass's version.** A cast to a superclass still dispatches to the override, and `super.super` doesn't exist.
**Code run through `super` calls your overrides.** A subclass that overrides a self-called method depends on the superclass's implementation, and can break when it changes.
**Overrides can't narrow access.** A subclass can only refuse an inherited method at run time, which breaks callers of the superclass.
**`protected` works across packages only through the subclass's own type**, and opens the member to the whole package.

blocks.text: Challenges

items: `AbstractCollection` documents that its `addAll` goes through `add`; `TreeSet` says nothing. Which other JDK classes document their self-calls, and would you subclass one that doesn't?
You maintain a library class that users already subclass, and you want `addAll` to stop calling `add` for speed. How do you find out whom you would break, and what do you ship instead?
A framework makes your entity extend its base class, and you need a count like the dashboard's. Where does the counter go so a framework upgrade can't change it?

blocks.text: Design Note: Why Fields Don't Dispatch

Java dispatches overridable instance methods and binds the rest without looking at the object: fields, static and private methods, `super` calls. A field read stays one instruction with no lookup, and a superclass's fields keep their meaning when a subclass adds one with the same name. The price is this page's opening bug. Keep fields `private` and expose behaviour through methods, which a subclass overrides on purpose.
